frames.note: Square opening. The mat hides 50 mm on every side.
Borderless. Full bleed to the opening.
No mat. Keep the subject away from the edge.

picks.title: The door that frames itself
points: Stand square to the door so both jambs stay vertical, then let the flowering branch fill the top third.
Expose for the pale wall; the blue only looks right when the paint reads bright, not muddied by shadow.
Leave a hand's width of wall below the step so the arch has something to sit on in the print.

picks.title: The table before anyone sits
points: Shoot from standing height with the near edge of the table parallel to the frame — a square crop forgives soft light, not a slanted row.
Let the two front chairs act as a gateway so the eye walks between them into the room.
Wait for window light to reach the far bowls rather than the near plates, and the centre of the table glows.

picks.title: A cat in the window seat
points: Centre the cat on the sill and give the same amount of shutter on each side; symmetry is the whole picture here.
Expose for the white paint and let the flowers go slightly rich — a blown sill flattens the window.
Keep one paw over the sill edge so the cat is standing on something instead of floating in the frame.

picks.title: Where the water draws the line
points: Find the point where the breaking wave meets the sand and put it on the lower third, never the middle.
Shoot at low tide from a high angle so the wet sand mirrors the sky and doubles the blue.
Keep the foam line unbroken across the frame; a single gap reads as a mistake at print size.

picks.title: One light left on
points: Shoot in the ten minutes after sunset, when the sky still holds colour and the lamp is the brightest thing in frame.
Crop the tower into the upper two thirds and leave room below for its reflection — the light needs somewhere to land.
Underexpose by a third of a stop so the lamp stays warm instead of burning a white hole in the sky.
